overview: This file traces the revival, foreign financing, construction, and financial condition of the Taiwan Electric Power Company’s Lake Candidius—now Sun Moon Lake—hydroelectric project between 1930 and 1932. It documents Japanese governmental approval for a foreign loan, American official interest in contracts and equipment sales, the eventual $22.5 million American bond issue, and later plans to refinance or repurchase those bonds because depreciation of the yen made gold-denominated interest costly. The papers also discuss—and reject—a supposed connection between the project and the 1930 Musha (Wushe) uprising, describe the project’s engineering and supply arrangements, and provide extensive statistical tables on the company’s finances, personnel, generating plants, and growing demand for electricity across colonial Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Reed on resumption of the Lake Candidius project
subfiles.about: Reports signs that the Lake Candidius hydroelectric project will resume after approval and foreign financing are obtained.
subfiles.summary: Reed reports the Governor-General favors resuming the Lake Candidius project, seeking Tokyo approval to raise ¥40 million via foreign loans within three years.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department request for information on hydroelectric contracts
subfiles.from: Robert J. Phillips, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.to: Wilbur J. Carr, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests details about contracting and purchasing opportunities arising from the Lake Candidius project.
subfiles.summary: Phillips relays Commerce's request for names of parties awarded hydroelectric construction contracts and machinery purchases, based on a Taihoku cable.
keywords: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Directs the consul to investigate commercial opportunities connected with the Lake Candidius project.
subfiles.summary: Department forwards Commerce's request to the Taihoku consul, ordering investigation of who could award construction contracts and purchase machinery, reply due as a despatch.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Forbes despatch on Taiwan Power Company loan
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch concerning cabinet approval of foreign borrowing for the Lake Jitsugetsudan project.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Forbes despatch on cabinet approval for the Taiwan Power Company's foreign loan for Lake Jitsugetsudan hydroelectric development.

subfiles.title: Excerpt from Forbes despatch on foreign financing and project criticism
subfiles.about: Discusses approval of a government-guaranteed foreign loan and doubts about the market for the project’s additional power.
subfiles.summary: Japan's cabinet approved roughly ¥45 million foreign borrowing by the Taiwan Power Company, an exception to its no-loan policy, as revised estimates cut costs; critics doubted the market could absorb more capacity, and press linked Morgan negotiations to indigenous unrest.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the history, financing, contracts, and engineering of the Jitsugetsutan project
subfiles.from: Charles S. Reed II, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed commercial and technical survey of the proposed resumption of the Lake Jitsugetsutan hydroelectric project.
subfiles.summary: Reed recounts the project’s organization in 1919, suspension in 1922, later engineering review, and approval for government-guaranteed foreign loans totaling up to 45.89 million yen. He argues that the Musha uprising was unrelated to the project and notes that the relatively small number of families displaced by the raised lake level had accepted resettlement sites. Contracts were likely to go to Japanese or Taiwanese firms, but remaining machinery purchases—handled through major Japanese trading houses—were expected to come largely from the United States. The despatch concludes with a detailed engineering description of river diversion, tunnels, dams, generating equipment, transmission lines, and revised specifications.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Reed telegram on the Governor-General’s resignation
subfiles.about: References a telegram assessing the effect of the Governor-General’s resignation on the hydroelectric project.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Reed's telegram judging the Governor-General's likely resignation after the Musha incident unlikely to affect the Lake Candidius project.

subfiles.title: Telegram on political resignations after the Musha incident
subfiles.about: Reports that expected resignations in Taiwan’s colonial administration should not disrupt the Candidius project.
subfiles.summary: Reed reports press claims the Governor-General will resign over the Musha incident, with most department heads possibly following, unlikely to affect the hydroelectric project.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to J. P. Morgan letter on Taiwan Electric Power bonds
subfiles.about: Records the sale of a major American bond issue intended to finance expansion of the Taiwan Electric Power Company.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a letter on a $22 million Taiwan Electric Power bond issue, purchased by Morgan and Yokohama Specie Bank.

subfiles.title: Corrected and duplicate telegrams on proposed bond repurchases
subfiles.from: Franklin, Amoy, relaying John L. Ketcham
subfiles.about: Reports a plan for the Taiwan Electric Power Company to borrow yen funds and repurchase its American gold bonds.
subfiles.summary: Franklin relays Ketcham's report that the company may borrow ¥20 million from Tokyo's Finance Department to repurchase bonds in Japan and discounted American-market bonds, cutting yen-exchange-burdened interest costs.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on the proposed internal loan
subfiles.about: Evaluates Ketcham’s November report on the company’s proposed twenty-million-yen refinancing loan.
subfiles.summary: Memo summarizes a plan for a Tokyo loan to retire 1931 American-floated gold debentures, finding no objection to limited circulation of the underlying report.

subfiles.title: Growth and Progress of the Taiwan Electric Power Company
subfiles.from: John L. Ketcham, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Presents a confidential survey of the company’s refinancing plans, construction progress, financial accounts, workforce, generating capacity, and electricity demand.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham explains the secret negotiations for a twenty-million-yen internal loan intended to repurchase the company’s dollar gold bonds and reduce the burden caused by yen depreciation. He reviews the $22.5 million American financing of the Sun Moon Lake project, reports construction about 35 percent complete in October 1932, and notes the exclusion of foreign construction bidders despite extensive use of American machinery. Translated company accounts show a large increase in debenture liabilities and liquid assets after the foreign loan, alongside falling profits and public complaints about high electricity rates. Extensive tables document personnel, plant capacity, output, and the rapid expansion and industrial uses of electric power, lighting, fans, and heating throughout Taiwan.

interest: Shows American finance in a Japanese colonial hydroelectric project, with construction reserved for Japanese/Taiwanese firms amid Musha-uprising risk fears.
